title: Finding Common Ground: The Importance of Place Attachment to Community Participation and Planning
authors: Lynne C. Manzo, Douglas D. Perkins, 2006
central_proposition: Place attachment, place identity, sense of community, and social capital are critical but often overlooked psychological dimensions that foster community development and participation across physical, social, political, and economic aspects, necessitating an integrated ecological framework for effective planning.

concept_definitions.name: place attachment
concept_definitions.definition: An affective bond between people and places, including different actors, social relationships, and places of varying scale.

concept_definitions.name: place identity
concept_definitions.definition: Dimensions of the self that develop in relation to the physical environment by means of a pattern of beliefs, preferences, feelings, values, and goals.

concept_definitions.name: sense of community
concept_definitions.definition: Feelings of membership or belongingness to a group, including an emotional connection based on a shared history, as well as shared interests or concerns.

concept_definitions.name: social capital
concept_definitions.definition: The extent and effectiveness of formal and informal human networks, as well as the impact of social ties on opportunities.

concept_definitions.name: empowerment
concept_definitions.definition: A mechanism by which people, organizations and communities gain mastery over their affairs.

concept_definitions.name: ecological perspective
concept_definitions.definition: An approach that engages multiple levels of analysis (individual, group/organization, community/neighborhood, and city/region/society) and examines multiple environmental domains (i.e., the physical, social, political and economic aspects of communities).

argument_structure: The paper identifies a critical gap in planning literature regarding the neglect of place-based psychological ties. It synthesizes concepts from environmental psychology (place attachment, place identity), community psychology/sociology (sense of community, social capital, empowerment), and planning theory (participation, conflict resolution). It argues that these psychological dimensions are fundamental drivers of community action and proposes an ecological framework to integrate these multi-level and multi-domain factors for a more holistic understanding of community dynamics and effective planning.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Emotional and cognitive bonds to place (place attachment, place identity) and social groups (sense of community, social capital) serve as intrinsic motivators for individuals and groups to engage in collective action, such as community participation, planning, and improvement. These bonds, when acknowledged and understood, can foster social cohesion, build consensus, and lead to empowerment. Conversely, ignoring or disrupting these bonds can lead to conflict, resistance, and community division, hindering successful planning and development efforts.

findings.antecedent: Place attachment and meaning
findings.consequent: Community participation and planning
findings.mechanism: Place attachments can motivate cooperative efforts to improve one's community.
findings.quote: Yet these attachments can motivate cooperative efforts to improve one's community.

findings.antecedent: Place attachments and meaning (intra-psychic phenomena)
findings.consequent: Behaviors toward places, participation in local planning efforts
findings.mechanism: Thoughts, feelings, and beliefs about local community places directly impact behaviors and willingness to participate.
findings.source: GROUNDING COMMUNITY PLANNING IN PLACE MEANING
findings.quote: Our thoughts, feelings, and beliefs about our local community places—what psychologists call 'intra-psychic' phenomena—impact our behaviors toward such places, thus influencing whether and how we might participate in local planning efforts.

findings.antecedent: Place attachments and sense of community
findings.consequent: Neighborhood revitalization efforts
findings.mechanism: These psychological bonds provide a foundation for community action.
findings.source: GROUNDING COMMUNITY PLANNING IN PLACE MEANING
findings.quote: a recent study by Brown, Perkins, and Brown (2003) found that place attachments and sense of community play a significant role in neighborhood revitalization efforts.

findings.antecedent: People's emotional relationships to places (place attachment)
findings.consequent: Involvement in local community
findings.mechanism: Emotional bonds to place are a core driver of engagement.
findings.source: Place Attachment—The Importance of Psychological Ties to Place
findings.quote: Such relationships are a critical aspect of people's involvement in their local community.

findings.antecedent: Place attachments
findings.consequent: Individual and group behavior, communities at large
findings.mechanism: Affective bonds to residence or neighborhood influence broader community dynamics.
findings.source: Place Attachment—The Importance of Psychological Ties to Place
findings.quote: Thus place attachments, in influencing individual and group behavior, affect communities at large.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Manzo (2003, 2005), Ahlbrandt (1984), Kasarda and Janowitz (1974), Taylor (1996), Brown, Perkins, and Brown (2003)

findings.antecedent: Place attachments
findings.consequent: Community clean-up and revitalization efforts
findings.mechanism: Emotional bonds motivate action to improve the environment.
findings.source: Place Attachment—The Importance of Psychological Ties to Place
findings.quote: It has also been linked to community clean-up and revitalization efforts (Brown, Perkins, and Brown 2003).

findings.antecedent: Romanticized notions of home and community, challenged ideals about community
findings.consequent: Difficulties, territorial conflicts
findings.mechanism: Discrepancy between ideals and reality, or conflicting attachments, can lead to negative outcomes.
findings.source: Place Attachment—The Importance of Psychological Ties to Place
findings.quote: attachments can also entrap or create territorial conflicts (Chawla 1992). For example, Manzo (2003, 2005) found how romanticized notions of home and community cause difficulties when they contrast with one's everyday experiences, or when ideals about community (either implicit or explicit) are challenged.

findings.antecedent: People's identity and values informed by significant places
findings.consequent: Engagement in those places (maintain, improve, respond to changes, stay)
findings.mechanism: Self-identity and values are tied to places, motivating action related to those places.
findings.source: Place Attachment—The Importance of Psychological Ties to Place
findings.quote: If people's identity and values are indeed informed by places they deem significant, then it follows that people's bonds with those places will impact their engagement in such places, whether it be to maintain or improve them, respond to changes within them, or simply to stay in that place (Pretty, Chipuer, and Bramston 2003).

findings.antecedent: Disruptions to place attachments (development projects, crime, relocation, environmental disasters)
findings.consequent: Sense of continuity, feelings of loss and alienation
findings.mechanism: Changes to the physical or social environment can break bonds and lead to negative emotional states.
findings.quote: disrupt place attachments, disturb a sense of continuity (Brown and Perkins 1992), and cause feelings of loss and alienation (Hummon 1992).

findings.antecedent: Properly recognized and understood feelings/reactions to disruption
findings.consequent: Citizen participation to rebuild a community
findings.mechanism: Addressing emotional responses to place changes can channel them into constructive collective action.
findings.quote: Tapping into such feelings and reactions to disruption can, if properly recognized and understood, help mobilize citizen participation to rebuild a community.

findings.antecedent: Unaddressed feelings/experiences of disruption
findings.consequent: Community division
findings.mechanism: Ignoring emotional responses to place changes can lead to internal community conflict.
findings.quote: Conversely, if such feelings and experiences are not well addressed, disruptions could divide a community.

findings.antecedent: Residents more attached to their community
findings.consequent: Higher levels of social cohesion and social control, less fear of crime, more outward signs of physical revitalization
findings.mechanism: Strong place bonds foster positive social dynamics and collective action for improvement and safety.
findings.quote: This is supported by recent research demonstrating that residents who are more attached to their community experience higher levels of social cohesion and social control and less fear of crime, while their neighborhoods have more outward signs of physical revitalization (Brown, Perkins, and Brown 2003).

findings.antecedent: Shared identity and place attachments (cultural connections, group histories, shared meanings)
findings.consequent: Success of urban landscapes, community planning and development efforts
findings.mechanism: Collective bonds to place provide a foundation for shared vision and action.
findings.quote: This literature examines cultural connections to, and expressions in, place as well as group histories and shared meanings of places. This is particularly critical for the success of urban landscapes, which by their nature house the 'public pasts' of many different groups who have a stake in a community (Hayden 1995).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Umemoto (2001), Zelinsky (1997), Hayden (1995), Abramson, Manzo, and Hou (forthcoming)

findings.antecedent: Acknowledged and discussed place meanings (among different stakeholders)
findings.consequent: Greater agreement on neighborhood plan, more satisfactory process
findings.mechanism: Understanding and incorporating diverse place meanings can resolve conflicts and build consensus.
findings.quote: However, once these place meanings were acknowledged and discussed, community leaders and planners made more concerted efforts to include the concerns of the different stakeholders and incorporate strategies that acknowledged those attachments. Competition among different ethnic groups for sociospatial expression greatly lessened as each group's role and heritage was acknowledged and incorporated into the plan. This led to greater agreement on the neighborhood plan and a more satisfactory process for all.

findings.antecedent: Understanding diverse meanings a neighborhood holds for its residents
findings.consequent: Creation of successful places, fostering action from emotionally invested parties
findings.mechanism: Recognizing varied place meanings allows for inclusive planning and motivates engagement.
findings.quote: The sharing of a common neighborhood space by diverse groups does not inevitably lead to a sense of community; therefore it is essential to understand the diverse meanings that a neighborhood holds for its residents in order to create successful places (Loukaitou-Sideris 1995). Such an understanding can also help foster action on the part of all parties who have an emotional stake in a place (Lukas 1985).

findings.antecedent: Residents expressing identity spatially (vernacular architecture, use of space)
findings.consequent: Sense of community, new attachments to place
findings.mechanism: Spatial expression of cultural identity reinforces social bonds and place connections.
findings.quote: Such practices can build a sense of community and create new attachments to place.

findings.antecedent: Residents more attached to their neighborhoods
findings.consequent: More likely to invest time and money, interact with neighbors, watch over communities
findings.mechanism: Strong place bonds motivate stewardship and social engagement.
findings.quote: Yet these very factors are related to place attachment, as those who are more attached to their neighborhoods are more likely to invest their time and money into the neighborhood. Those who are more attached to their neighborhoods also interact more with neighbors and watch over their communities more. Such activities stem from, and also create, further social cohesion, no matter how diverse the community members might be (Brown, Perkins, and Brown 2003).

findings.antecedent: People's attachments to place
findings.consequent: Sense of community
findings.mechanism: Emotional bonds to physical places and social groups are often co-occurring and mutually reinforcing.
findings.quote: People's attachments to place are often intertwined with their sense of community (Pretty, Chipuer, and Bramson 2003).

findings.antecedent: Attachment to the neighborhood
findings.consequent: Development of a sense of community among neighbors
findings.mechanism: A primary bond to the physical setting can facilitate the formation of social bonds.
findings.quote: Rivlin's (1987) study of a Brooklyn neighborhood found that attachment to the neighborhood served as a precondition for the development of a sense of community among neighbors.

findings.antecedent: Sense of community and place attachment
findings.consequent: Participation (behavioral manifestation)
findings.mechanism: Both types of bonds motivate active engagement.
findings.quote: Moreover, both sense of community and place attachment manifest themselves behaviorally in participation.

findings.antecedent: Sense of community
findings.consequent: Citizen participation, other positive individual and neighborhood outcomes
findings.mechanism: Social cohesion and belonging foster active engagement and positive collective results.
findings.quote: Because sense of community is linked to citizen participation (Cuba and Hummon 1993; Perkins, Brown, and Taylor 1996) and other positive individual and neighborhood outcomes, creating and fostering a sense of community has become a key goal in planning practice (Morris 1996).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cuba and Hummon (1993), Perkins, Brown, and Taylor (1996)

findings.antecedent: Careful explorations of place meanings, attachments, and identity
findings.consequent: Successful revitalization projects, positive community outcomes
findings.mechanism: Understanding and incorporating deep-seated place values ensures plans align with community needs and motivations, fostering success.
findings.quote: Such revitalization projects—rooted in careful explorations of place meanings, attachments, and identity—are still uncommon. However, they are essential to understand better so that we may learn how such processes impact community planning, preservation, and development, as well as how they can lead to positive community outcomes.

findings.antecedent: Individual identity and power relations
findings.consequent: Everyday uses and meanings of place
findings.mechanism: Social and political structures shape how individuals experience and interpret places.
findings.source: THE POLITICS OF PLACE AND PLACE ATTACHMENT
findings.quote: A close examination of place attachments reveals how individual identity and power relations manifest themselves in the everyday uses and meanings of place (Devine-Wright and Lyons 1997; Dixon and Durrheim 2000; Manzo 2003).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Devine-Wright and Lyons (1997), Dixon and Durrheim (2000), Manzo (2003)

findings.antecedent: Place attachments, place meaning, and larger sociopolitical reality
findings.consequent: Political action
findings.mechanism: Personal and collective bonds to place are intertwined with power dynamics and can drive political engagement.
findings.source: THE POLITICS OF PLACE AND PLACE ATTACHMENT
findings.quote: In making this argument, scholars draw a critical connection among place attachments, place meaning, and the larger sociopolitical reality in which we live, while connecting each to political action (Keith and Pile 1993).

findings.antecedent: Place attachments (particularly health-, property-, place-related anxieties)
findings.consequent: Community division and immobilization
findings.mechanism: Unaddressed emotional responses to place-related concerns can lead to internal conflict and prevent collective action.
findings.source: THE POLITICS OF PLACE AND PLACE ATTACHMENT
findings.quote: Consequently, environmental and community psychology studies on the intersection of the politics of place and place attachments warrant further exploration.

findings.antecedent: Common interest in health and neighborhood (in response to environmental problems)
findings.consequent: Partnership approach, mobilization toward action, empowerment
findings.mechanism: Shared concerns about place can unite diverse parties and catalyze collective action.
findings.source: THE POLITICS OF PLACE AND PLACE ATTACHMENT
findings.quote: In such cases, place attachments can be used to foster a partnership approach as different parties find common interest in their health and their neighborhood. When residents are able to take control of the situation themselves and identify common interests and targets, they are more likely to be mobilized toward action and be empowered (Edelstein 2003; Rich et al. 1995; Kemmis 1990).

findings.antecedent: Place attachments
findings.consequent: Community conflict
findings.mechanism: Conflicting emotional bonds to place can lead to disagreements and opposition.
findings.source: Place Attachment and Conflict in Community Planning and Development
findings.quote: While place attachments can form the basis for cooperation and community action, they can also lie at the root of community conflict (Forester 1987).

findings.antecedent: Policy makers framing community responses as 'NIMBY'
findings.consequent: Undermining legitimacy of opponents' views, limited utility in explaining responses to environmental change
findings.mechanism: Labeling opposition as irrational ignores the valid emotional and symbolic concerns tied to place.
findings.source: Place Attachment and Conflict in Community Planning and Development
findings.quote: Devine-Wright (2003) argues that policy makers and commentators who frame community responses in terms of a NIMBY reaction typically depict people as inflexible and irrationally opposed to change, while assuming self-interested and egoistic motives for behavior. ... He argues that this has limited utility in accurately explaining the 'important emotional and symbolic character' of community members' response to local environmental change (p. 2).

findings.antecedent: Careful understanding of community members' place attachments
findings.consequent: Better understanding of social acceptability of change
findings.mechanism: Understanding the emotional bonds allows for more nuanced assessment of community reactions to change.
findings.source: Place Attachment and Conflict in Community Planning and Development
findings.quote: A careful understanding of the place attachments of community members can provide a better understanding of the social acceptability of change.

findings.antecedent: Understanding that place meaning is socially determined (not intrinsic)
findings.consequent: Acceptance of diverse meanings as valid, airing problems, discussing solutions, depersonalized conflicts, increased cooperation
findings.mechanism: A social constructionist view of place meaning allows for respectful dialogue and collaborative problem-solving.
findings.source: Place Attachment and Conflict in Community Planning and Development
findings.quote: They argue that once it is understood that meaning is not intrinsic to a place but is socially determined, then it becomes possible to accept diverse meanings as valid, air problems, and discuss solutions. In this way, conflicts are depersonalized and viewpoints on issues are less likely to be seen as moral imperatives; hence, cooperation becomes more possible.

findings.antecedent: Consensus-building strategies (long-term, face-to-face discussions, exploring assumptions, acknowledging different viewpoints)
findings.consequent: Agreement on strategies/plans/policies/actions, uncovering symbolic values/place meanings/attachments
findings.mechanism: Collaborative dialogue allows for deeper understanding of underlying values and emotional connections, leading to shared solutions.
findings.source: Place Attachment and Conflict in Community Planning and Development
findings.quote: It is not coincidental that the successful consensus-building strategies that Innes advocates involve longer-term, face-to-face discussions that seek agreement among different community members and stakeholders, as it is through these processes that the symbolic values, place meanings, and attachments can be uncovered.

findings.antecedent: Explicit explorations of place meaning and attachments among stakeholders (in consensus building)
findings.consequent: Shared values ('common ground'), development of social capital
findings.mechanism: Directly addressing emotional bonds and meanings fosters shared understanding and strengthens social networks.
findings.source: Place Attachment and Conflict in Community Planning and Development
findings.quote: This can help move community members toward what Kemmis (1995) calls 'the common ground of shared values' in the local community. Such a process can also facilitate the development of what social scientists call social capital (Flora and Flora 1996).

findings.antecedent: Place attachments and social capital
findings.consequent: Community assets
findings.mechanism: Both represent valuable resources for community well-being and action.
findings.source: Social Capital and Place Attachment: Understanding Community Assets
findings.quote: As we have seen, both social capital and place attachments are community assets.

findings.antecedent: Strong social capital and consensus (in communities)
findings.consequent: Environmental problems can catalyze community action
findings.mechanism: Existing social resources allow communities to focus on shared assets to address problems, even with differing place values.
findings.source: Social Capital and Place Attachment: Understanding Community Assets
findings.quote: In places where social capital and consensus are already strong, environmental problems can catalyze community action as residents focus on those assets they share as neighbors to help address the problem, even if their particular place-based values and attachments differ (Perkins, Brown, and Taylor 1996).

findings.antecedent: Shared investment in local environment and its value (in strife-ridden communities)
findings.consequent: Community members come together in formal associations, social capital develops
findings.mechanism: A common stake in the physical environment provides a basis for collective action and network formation, even amidst conflict.
findings.source: Social Capital and Place Attachment: Understanding Community Assets
findings.quote: Conversely, where conflicts already exist, it is easier for community members to come together in formal associations when they focus on their shared investment in the local environment and its value in their lives as residents. In that more formally structured way, social capital can develop in strife-ridden communities.

findings.antecedent: Sense of community (trust in neighbors)
findings.consequent: Informal neighboring activity, participation in formally organized neighborhood groups
findings.mechanism: Feelings of belonging and trust drive both casual and formal social engagement.
findings.source: Table 1, Social Capital and Place Attachment: Understanding Community Assets
findings.quote: As Table 1 indicates, the key informal community-related cognition is sense of community, or trust in one's neighbors, which helps motivate both informal neighboring activity and participation in formally organized neighborhood groups.

findings.antecedent: Empowerment (sense of efficacy of collective action)
findings.consequent: Organized citizen participation
findings.mechanism: Belief in collective agency translates into active involvement.
findings.source: Table 1, Social Capital and Place Attachment: Understanding Community Assets
findings.quote: Formally-oriented community-focused cognitions relate to empowerment, or a sense of efficacy of collective action, which corresponds behaviorally to organized citizen participation.

findings.antecedent: Social capital (newcomers' organizing skills, vitality)
findings.consequent: Integration into community, resolution of conflicts (e.g., Wal-Mart debate)
findings.mechanism: Recognizing and leveraging diverse forms of social capital can bridge divides and foster collaboration.
findings.source: Social Capital and Place Attachment: Understanding Community Assets
findings.quote: In this case, the newcomers had organizing skills and added new vitality to the community; these could be seen as an important new resource to be integrated into the community (Flora and Flora 1996).

findings.antecedent: Shared, mutually agreed-upon value in the neighborhood (environmental capital)
findings.consequent: Social capital built, public life reclaimed
findings.mechanism: A common appreciation for the physical environment can serve as a foundation for social cohesion and civic engagement.
findings.source: Social Capital and Place Attachment: Understanding Community Assets
findings.quote: Conversely, in cases where there exists a shared, mutually agreed-upon value in the neighborhood, the environment can be the resource on which social capital is built. Kemmis (1995) argues for a greater focus on the commonly shared environmental capital of communities to stem what he views as the demise of public life. He claims that public life can be reclaimed only by understanding and practicing connections to real, identifiable places.

findings.antecedent: Place identity (one's sense of self informed by neighborhood places)
findings.consequent: Cognitive dimension of community interaction
findings.mechanism: Self-concept is shaped by the physical environment.
findings.quote: On the cognitive dimension, there is both place identity and community identity (i.e., one's sense of self as informed by neighborhood places and by social interactions/neighboring respectively).

findings.antecedent: Place attachment (emotional relationship to neighborhood/specific places)
findings.consequent: Affective dimension of community interaction
findings.mechanism: Emotional bonds to physical places are a core component of how people feel about their community.
findings.quote: The affective dimension refers to one's emotional relationship to the neighborhood or specific places within it (this takes the form of place attachments)...

findings.antecedent: Sense of community (emotional relationships with neighbors/local community groups)
findings.consequent: Affective dimension of community interaction
findings.mechanism: Emotional bonds to social groups are a core component of how people feel about their community.
findings.quote: ...as well as one's emotional relationships with neighbors and other local community groups (this takes the form of sense of community).

findings.antecedent: Place-focused action (participation in community planning, preservation, development)
findings.consequent: Behavioral dimension of community interaction
findings.mechanism: Active engagement in shaping the physical environment is a key community behavior.
findings.quote: Finally, the behavioral dimension includes participation in community planning, preservation, and development efforts (in regard to place-focused action)...

findings.antecedent: Socially oriented behavior (neighboring, crime prevention, social activities)
findings.consequent: Behavioral dimension of community interaction
findings.mechanism: Social interactions and collective efforts for social well-being are key community behaviors.
findings.quote: ...as well as engaging in neighboring and other social activities (in regard to socially oriented behavior).

findings.antecedent: Participation
findings.consequent: Sense of empowerment among community members
findings.mechanism: Active involvement in community processes fosters a sense of control and agency.
findings.quote: An examination of the political underpinnings of place attachments and social capital reveal the ways in which participation can enable a sense of empowerment to emerge among community members.

findings.antecedent: Place attachments, social capital, action
findings.consequent: Community empowerment
findings.mechanism: These factors are intertwined and mediate each other, leading to collective mastery over community affairs.
findings.quote: Empowerment, defined by Rapoport (1987) as 'a mechanism by which people, organizations and communities gain mastery over their affairs' (p. 122), illustrates the connection among place attachments, social capital, and action. Indeed, it may be a mediating factor that draws them all together.

findings.antecedent: Shared values and emotional ties to others
findings.consequent: More meaningful/sustainable bonds, social power built
findings.mechanism: Deep social and emotional connections form the basis of strong, lasting relationships and collective influence.
findings.quote: They claim that 'relationships based on shared values and emotional ties to others produce more meaningful/sustainable bonds than emotional reaction to community issues alone' (Speer and Hughey 1995, p. 733). These studies of empowerment demonstrate that social power is built on the strength of interpersonal relationships among those working toward a common goal (Perkins 1995; Rich et al. 1995; Speer and Hughey 1995; Florin and Wandersman 1990).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Speer and Hughey (1995), Perkins (1995), Rich et al. (1995), Florin and Wandersman (1990)

findings.antecedent: Shared valued and emotional ties to places
findings.consequent: Strengthen social relationships, collective community action
findings.mechanism: Common emotional bonds to the physical environment reinforce social connections and collective action.
findings.quote: We also argue that shared emotional ties to places strengthen social relationships and collective community action even further.

findings.antecedent: Communities facing environmental problems (threats)
findings.consequent: 'Enabling response' (citizens come together, common purpose, new responses)
findings.mechanism: A shared crisis can mobilize collective action and transform powerlessness into empowerment.
findings.quote: In particular, communities facing environmental problems can develop an 'enabling response' in which citizens come together to confront a crisis (Edelstein 2003). Here, previously disempowering conditions such as an individual's sense of powerlessness, or inability to escape a hazardous situation, can be transformed through collective action, in which individuals develop a common purpose and create new responses to meet the challenges they face (Rich et al. 1995).

findings.antecedent: Place attachments and social capital (key ingredients)
findings.consequent: Effective community-based action, community households
findings.mechanism: These bonds are fundamental resources for successful collective action in housing and community development.
findings.quote: Based upon this phenomenon, the authors developed the concept of 'community households,' which identifies place attachments and social capital as key ingredients of effective community-based action.

findings.antecedent: Individual-level place attachment/identity
findings.consequent: Individual-level physical environmental domain phenomena
findings.mechanism: Personal bonds to place are a key individual experience of the physical environment.
findings.quote: Addressing individual-level issues related to the physical environmental domain would include an exploration of place attachments and place identity...

findings.antecedent: Individual-level sense of community/community attachment/neighboring behavior
findings.consequent: Individual-level social domain phenomena
findings.mechanism: Personal feelings of belonging and social interactions are key individual experiences of the social environment.
findings.quote: ...while in the social domain one could study sense of community and community-level attachments and neighboring behavior.

findings.antecedent: Individual-level political engagement/empowerment
findings.consequent: Individual-level political domain phenomena
findings.mechanism: Individual agency and participation are key political experiences.
findings.quote: In the political domain, individual-level phenomena include political engagement and empowerment.

findings.antecedent: Individual-level decisions about where to buy/develop property, investments in maintenance/improvements, financial contributions
findings.consequent: Individual-level economic domain phenomena
findings.mechanism: Personal economic choices reflect and influence the economic environment.
findings.quote: In the economic domain, it includes decisions about where to buy and develop property, investments in maintenance and improvements, and financial contributions to community organizations.

findings.antecedent: Social group/neighborhood-level participation in community events (clean-ups, planning projects)
findings.consequent: Social group/neighborhood-level physical domain phenomena
findings.mechanism: Collective action shapes the physical environment.
findings.quote: For example, at the social group and neighborhood levels, we can examine people's participation in community events like neighborhood clean-ups and planning projects in the physical domain...

findings.antecedent: Social group/neighborhood-level social cohesion, networking, social capital
findings.consequent: Social group/neighborhood-level social domain phenomena
findings.mechanism: Group-level social dynamics are key aspects of the social environment.
findings.quote: ...and examine the nature and degree of social cohesion, networking, and social capital (in the social domain)...

findings.antecedent: Social group/neighborhood-level empowerment, fundraising, resource sharing
findings.consequent: Social group/neighborhood-level political and economic domain phenomena
findings.mechanism: Collective agency and resource management are key political and economic group-level dynamics.
findings.quote: ...while studying the degree or process of empowerment, fundraising, and resource sharing in the political and economic domain, respectively.

findings.antecedent: City/region/societal-level macro-structural forces (demographic shifts, diversity, social services, political/economic institutions/policies)
findings.consequent: City/region/societal-level phenomena
findings.mechanism: Broad societal forces shape community dynamics at higher levels.
findings.quote: The city/region/societal level of analysis would examine macro-structural forces such as demographic shifts and diversity, social services, and the impact of political and economic institutions and policies.

findings.antecedent: Focus on place (clean-up of vacant lot)
findings.consequent: Attention from media/city hall, 'winnable' issue, tangible evidence of collective power, physical rallying point, vision of better neighborhood, justified attachment
findings.mechanism: A concrete, place-based issue can mobilize resources, demonstrate collective efficacy, and reinforce community bonds.
findings.source: Community-driven Projects with an Ecological Perspective
findings.quote: It is no accident that DSNI started with a focus on place—the clean up of a vacant lot that had become an illegal dumping ground. This provided residents with (a) attention from the media and city hall; (b) a 'winnable' issue and almost immediate success; (c) tangible evidence of their collective power; (d) a physical rallying point for mobilizing community action; and (e) a vision of a better, safer, more attractive neighborhood that justified their attachment to it (Medoff and Sklar 1994).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Medoff and Sklar (1994) - Dudley Street Neighborhood Initiative (DSNI)

findings.antecedent: Residents' attachments to residence
findings.consequent: Mobilization, claims on legal owners/public agencies, sense of empowerment, sense of social ownership
findings.mechanism: Personal bonds to home motivate collective action to assert rights and gain control.
findings.source: Community-driven Projects with an Ecological Perspective
findings.quote: Here, residents also mobilized based on their attachments to their residence, and they made claims on the legal owners of the neglected buildings where they lived as well as on the public agencies responsible for the neighborhood. This, in turn, provided residents with a sense of empowerment and helped them develop a sense of social ownership.

findings.antecedent: Place attachment, place identity, sense of community
findings.consequent: Resources for neighborhoods to withstand displacement (abandonment, gentrification)
findings.mechanism: These psychological bonds act as protective factors against negative social and economic forces.
findings.source: Community-driven Projects with an Ecological Perspective
findings.quote: This work demonstrates that place attachment, place identity, and sense of community are resources for neighborhoods that require cultivation to withstand the social and economic forces that can lead to displacement through property abandonment or gentrification (Saegert 2000; see also Pretty, Chipuer, and Bramson 2003).

findings.antecedent: Community social networks and intentional political pressures (to address abandoned buildings)
findings.consequent: Physical environmental problem addressed, economic consequences for low-income community
findings.mechanism: Organized social and political capital can be leveraged to solve physical environmental issues with broader economic benefits.

findings.quote: What was most unusual about this project, and perhaps its greatest value as an exemplary model, was how interdisciplinary the action-research team was. Two community psychologists (Speer and Peterson), three urban planners (Ontkush, Schmitt, and Rengert), an economist (Rahman), and a sociologist (Jackson) collaborated closely across multiple disciplinary divides to work together with community leaders and organizers.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Higher levels of place attachment and sense of community will predict greater individual participation in neighborhood planning and improvement efforts.

Communities where place meanings and attachments are explicitly explored and integrated into planning processes will exhibit higher rates of consensus building and successful project implementation compared to those where they are not.
Disruptions to place attachments (e.g., through redevelopment or environmental hazards) will lead to increased feelings of loss and alienation, and if unaddressed, to greater community conflict.
Interdisciplinary planning teams that integrate environmental psychology, community psychology, and planning expertise will achieve more holistic and effective community development outcomes.
The presence of shared place-based values and emotional ties will positively correlate with the development of social capital and collective action in communities.
bridge_warrants: Connects environmental psychology's focus on individual place experience with community psychology's focus on social dynamics and planning's focus on macro-structural forces.
Argues that psychological ties to place are a 'common ground' for diverse residents and planners, bridging individual experience with collective action.
Proposes that understanding place attachments can transform 'NIMBY' reactions from irrational opposition to legitimate concerns, facilitating conflict resolution.
methodological_critiques: Environmental psychologists often focus on individual experiences and meaning, neglecting the collective nature of these phenomena.
Community psychologists address community development and social capital but often overlook individual experience or place-based theories.
Planners and community designers tend to examine neighborhood-level dynamics and macro-structural forces, often neglecting personal experiences of place and attachments.
A common perception among practitioners is that social science research on place meanings and psychosocial dynamics is a 'luxury' they cannot afford.
model_structure: The paper proposes an 'Ecological Framework for Community Planning and Development' structured as a matrix. It integrates four 'Environmental Domains (or Forms of Capital)'—Physical, Social, Political, and Economic—with four 'Levels of Analysis'—Individual, Social group/organization, Neighborhood, and City/region/society. Each cell in the matrix identifies specific phenomena to study (e.g., 'Place attachment/identity' at the Individual-Physical level, 'Sense of community' at the Individual-Social level, 'Participatory planning and design' at the Social group/organization-Physical level).
limitations: The current lack of interdisciplinary collaboration hinders a holistic understanding of community phenomena.
The perception among practitioners that social science research on place meanings and psychosocial dynamics is a 'luxury' limits its application.

paper_metadata.title: Finding Common Ground: The Importance of Place Attachment to Community Participation and Planning
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Finding Common Ground: The Importance of Place Attachment to Community Participation and Planning
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This article draws connections between the environmental and community psychology literature on place attachment and meaning with the theory, research, and practice of community participation and planning. Each area of inquiry has much to offer the other, yet few links have been made between them. Typically, literature on place attachment focuses on individual feelings and experiences and has not placed these bonds in the larger, sociopolitical context in which planners operate. Conversely, the community planning literature emphasizes participation and empowerment, but overlooks emotional connections to place. Yet these attachments can motivate cooperative efforts to improve one’s community. Literature across disciplines is examined and synthesized to develop a framework for understanding the psychological dimensions of people’s interactions with community. An ecological model is then proposed that integrates multiple environmental domains and analysis levels. This model can accommodate place attachments and meaning as well as social and political aspects of community participation.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Conceptual Framework of Place Attachment and Community Participation
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Place attachment, encompassing emotional, cognitive, and functional bonds to a place, is a critical antecedent that fosters a sense of responsibility and belonging, thereby motivating individuals to engage in community participation and planning processes.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper proposes a multi-step mechanism where place attachment leads to community participation through the development of place identity, responsibility, and motivation.
